question.text: Of the three constitutional forms permitted for an AIF, the TRUST structure dominates the Indian Cat III AIF market. Which reason is the PRIMARY driver of this dominance?

answer.text: Trust form allows unlimited leverage unlike LLP and company forms
Trusts offer operational flexibility, bespoke governance via the Trust Deed, lower compliance cost, and investor confidentiality
Only a trust form allows SEBI registration under AIF Regulations; LLP and company forms are disallowed in practice
The Indian Trusts Act, 1882 exempts AIF trusts from maintaining books of accounts

explanation.text: The Logic: The trust is dominant because it allows bespoke governance (drafted in the trust deed), is lightly regulated outside SEBI, has lower compliance cost than LLP/company, and keeps investor names out of the public domain (LLPs file investor details on the MCA portal). The workbook explicitly states this is why the majority of Indian AIFs use the trust form. The Trap: Option A conflates leverage rules (which depend on AIF category, not form) with legal form. Option C is wrong — all three forms are permitted. Option D is a fabricated exemption; trust still maintains books. Cross-Exam Context: This is shared across XIX-A/B/C/D and also covered in XXI-B for PMS vs AIF structural choice questions. Manager's Pro-Tip: For a Cat III desk the trust form also makes side-pocketing and series-of-units for HWM much cleaner to administer versus an LLP, which would require LLP-deed amendments for every unit class.
